about: Idioms, dichos and slang for characters to use, one a visit, glossed with the picture then the meaning (docs/mix.md → Idioms; Josh, 2026-11-13: "Idioms stick", "we might favor shotter and common", "slang is very common in Mexico", "start the list and I'll get youo edits later"). Chosen from Seven Keys, Mexican Spanish Word Power, the Compendio temático de dichos y refranes, Iribarren's El porqué de los dichos, refranes lists, food dichos (México Destinos, México Desconocido) and Los dichos de Jesús: common in Mexico, 2 to 6 words (slang any length), not already in syllabus.json; 50 Mexican-only dichos, 25 shared, 25 slang, plus common biblical sayings. Only the dichos come from the sources; pictures, meanings and situations are our own words. Not checked by a Mexican yet: edits to come. common: very common | common; group: dicho (Mexican) | shared | slang | biblical.

idioms.picture: to a good understander, few words
idioms.meaning: a sharp person gets the hint; no need to spell it out
idioms.fits: hinting at something instead of saying it
idioms.origin: high-context talk: much is left unsaid and you're trusted to read it

idioms.picture: giving and giving, little bird flying
idioms.meaning: pay first, then you get it; a fair swap on the spot
idioms.fits: a market stall: money in one hand, goods in the other

idioms.text: de lengua me como un taco
idioms.picture: I'll eat a tongue taco out of words
idioms.fits: someone boasting they could easily do something
someone drops out of a shared meal

idioms.text: a fuerza, ni los zapatos entran
idioms.picture: by force, not even shoes go on
idioms.meaning: you can't force things, or people
better to keep your mouth shut
idioms.fits: someone is about to say something unwise

idioms.picture: to load the little corpse on someone
idioms.meaning: to pin the blame on someone

idioms.fits: a child nagging, a neighbour's noise

idioms.picture: to set the dogs on someone
idioms.meaning: to hound or harass someone; in Mexico "echarle los perros" usually means to flirt with someone
idioms.fits: in Mexico, a friend clearly hitting on someone at a party
idioms.origin: dogs were once set on bulls that refused to charge; the book also suggests the conquistadors' war dogs

idioms.meaning: someone criticising a fault they have
idioms.fits: someone calls another lazy or late

idioms.text: el que la sigue la mata (el que sigue la liebre la mata)
idioms.picture: whoever chases the hare kills it
idioms.meaning: persistence wins in the end; Mexico says "el que la sigue la consigue"
idioms.fits: encouraging someone who keeps applying for jobs
idioms.origin: it comes from hunting: the hunter who keeps after the hare is the one who catches it

idioms.text: El que no tranza, no avanza
idioms.picture: who doesn't cheat doesn't get ahead
idioms.meaning: Cynically: cheating is how you advance.
to be very hard to understand or do

idioms.origin: the book's author approves of old-fashioned discipline

idioms.fits: Mother's Day (10 May), a mother's cooking
a favourite dish, hobby or skill

idioms.text: No soy monedita de oro (pa' caerles bien a todos)
idioms.picture: I'm not a gold coin, to please everyone
idioms.fits: someone disliked by a few; a well-known song line

idioms.picture: to take the turn around it
idioms.fits: someone dodges a chore or a person

idioms.text: Una sopa de su propio chocolate
idioms.picture: a soup of your own chocolate
idioms.meaning: a taste of your own medicine
to pry into someone's private affairs

idioms.text: Asustar con el petate del muerto
idioms.picture: scaring someone with the dead man's mat
idioms.meaning: trying to frighten with an empty threat
hardship never goes beyond what you can bear

idioms.text: el hombre propone, Dios dispone (y llega el diablo y todo lo descompone)
idioms.picture: man proposes, God decides, and the devil comes and wrecks it all
idioms.fits: when plans fall through, laughing it off
idioms.origin: little faith in control over events, so promises stay loose

idioms.fits: asked about a hobby or talent

idioms.meaning: furious, boiling with anger or passion
idioms.fits: someone furious; also the novel and film

idioms.meaning: someone asking a favour yet making demands
idioms.fits: someone asks for help and complains about it

idioms.picture: he left him like a sweet potato
idioms.meaning: he gave him a severe telling-off or beating

idioms.fits: a foreign-born person who loves everything Mexican

idioms.picture: don't make yourself into a ring-shaped bread

idioms.text: O todos coludos o todos rabones
idioms.picture: either all long-tailed or all bob-tailed
you look like a pumpkin seed on the griddle

idioms.text: Según el sapo, es la pedrada
idioms.meaning: respond in proportion to the problem
idioms.fits: sizing up a task or a person

idioms.text: A lo que te truje Chencha
idioms.picture: what I brought you here for, Chencha
to have your party watered down

idioms.meaning: let's drop it, leave it there
idioms.fits: ending an argument or a deal: "ahí muere"

idioms.text: Al peor puerco, la mejor guayaba
idioms.picture: to the worst pig, the best guava
idioms.meaning: the least deserving get the best things
idioms.fits: a lazy person gets lucky; an unpleasant man with a lovely wife

idioms.text: Ante la duda, la más peluda
idioms.meaning: when unsure, play the biggest tile

idioms.text: Aquí el que menos corre, vuela
idioms.meaning: everyone here is quick and sharp

idioms.picture: only my pork rinds crackle here

idioms.meaning: here I'm in charge; what I say goes
idioms.fits: a fonda owner or a grandmother running her kitchen

idioms.meaning: to make a scene, throw a fit
idioms.fits: a customer makes a scene in a shop; a child's tantrum

idioms.meaning: a good meal makes you happy
a new love cures an old one
idioms.fits: someone dates soon after a breakup
idioms.origin: from Cicero; carpenters push out a stuck nail with another

idioms.text: Al que madruga, Dios lo ayuda
idioms.fits: encouraging someone to get up early for the market
idioms.origin: the joke reply (the one who lost the purse got up even earlier) already appears in 16th-century tales

idioms.picture: we see faces, we don't know hearts
idioms.meaning: you can't know what people really feel
idioms.fits: someone turned out different than expected

idioms.text: El que mucho abarca, poco aprieta
idioms.picture: who grabs a lot holds little tightly
idioms.meaning: take on too much and you'll do it badly
idioms.fits: someone takes on too many projects
a friend recovers fast; teasing someone who turns up unharmed

idioms.text: Nadie es profeta en su tierra
idioms.picture: no one is a prophet in his own land
idioms.fits: someone famous abroad but ignored at home
idioms.origin: Jesus' words when his own town of Nazareth scorned him

idioms.text: otra vez la burra al trigo
idioms.picture: the donkey back at the wheat again
idioms.meaning: there they go again, the same mistake

idioms.picture: to be flour from another sack
a good listener needs few words
idioms.meaning: a hint is enough for the wise

idioms.text: dar en el clavo (antes, dar en el hito)
idioms.fits: someone guesses exactly what's wrong with your car
idioms.origin: either from blacksmiths shoeing horses, who hit the shoe far more than the nail, or from an old game of throwing rings or coins at a peg stuck in the ground

idioms.picture: from such a stick, such a splinter
idioms.fits: a child acts like a parent
someone says nothing to a proposal

idioms.text: El que la hace, la paga
idioms.picture: whoever does it pays for it

idioms.text: El que nada debe, nada teme
idioms.meaning: an honest person has nothing to fear
idioms.fits: someone is accused but stays calm

idioms.text: El que no llora no mama
idioms.picture: the baby who doesn't cry doesn't nurse
idioms.meaning: the squeaky wheel gets the grease
idioms.fits: encouraging someone to ask or complain

idioms.meaning: time is valuable; don't waste it

idioms.text: En boca cerrada no entran moscas
idioms.picture: flies don't enter a closed mouth
idioms.meaning: keep quiet and stay out of trouble

idioms.picture: to enter with the right foot
idioms.fits: starting the new year or a new job
idioms.origin: from the old superstition of always stepping off with the right foot when starting a journey

idioms.meaning: to be hard; to be intense
what a drag; I can't be bothered

idioms.fits: "no te agüites" to cheer someone up
a sore loser after a match

idioms.meaning: overused, worn out (a joke, a song)
to treat someone, pay for them
a fixer who sells shortcuts at offices (also people smuggler)

idioms.text: el que esté libre de pecado, que tire la primera piedra
idioms.picture: whoever has no sin, throw the first stone
idioms.meaning: nobody is clean enough to condemn others
idioms.fits: someone gossips harshly about another's mistake
idioms.origin: John 8: a crowd ready to stone a woman; Jesus tells the sinless one to start, and they leave

idioms.text: ver la paja en el ojo ajeno (y no la viga en el propio)
idioms.picture: seeing a speck of straw in someone else's eye and missing the beam in your own
idioms.meaning: criticising small faults in others while ignoring your own big ones
idioms.fits: someone complains about a neighbour who has the same habit
idioms.origin: Matthew 7, Sermon on the Mount

idioms.text: el hijo pródigo (volvió el hijo pródigo)
idioms.meaning: someone who comes back after a long absence, often after going astray; said warmly or teasingly
idioms.fits: a regular reappears after months away
idioms.origin: Luke 15: a son squanders his inheritance, comes home broke, and his father throws a feast

idioms.meaning: a stranger who stops to help
idioms.fits: someone helped a stranger with a flat tyre or a fall
idioms.origin: Luke 10: a man beaten on the road is passed by a priest and a Levite and helped by a despised Samaritan

idioms.meaning: the humble or late can end up ahead; also a joke for whoever arrives last
idioms.fits: the last to arrive gets served first
idioms.origin: Matthew 19–20 and Mark 10, Jesus on the kingdom

idioms.text: muchos son los llamados y pocos los escogidos
idioms.picture: many are called, few are chosen
idioms.fits: a hard audition, a competition, a job opening
idioms.origin: Matthew 20 and 22, the end of two parables

idioms.text: el que tenga oídos, que oiga
idioms.picture: whoever has ears, let him hear
idioms.meaning: I've said it; whoever understands, take note (a pointed hint)
idioms.fits: dropping a hint everyone in the room gets
idioms.origin: Jesus's closing line after parables (Matthew 13, Luke 8) and in Revelation

idioms.text: que tu mano izquierda no sepa lo que hace la derecha / la mano izquierda no sabe lo que hace la derecha
idioms.picture: the left hand not knowing what the right is doing
idioms.meaning: give quietly, without showing off; now mostly said of a disorganised office where nobody coordinates
idioms.fits: two counters at the town hall give opposite answers
idioms.origin: Matthew 6, on giving alms in secret

idioms.text: volver a nacer / nacer de nuevo
idioms.meaning: to survive a close call, or start life afresh
idioms.fits: after a near-accident or a recovery
idioms.origin: John 3: Jesus tells Nicodemus a person must be born again

idioms.picture: like manna falling from the sky
idioms.meaning: an unexpected help that arrives just when needed
idioms.fits: rain after a drought, a refund at month's end
idioms.origin: Exodus 16: bread falls from the sky for the Israelites in the desert

idioms.text: por los siglos de los siglos
idioms.picture: for the centuries of the centuries
idioms.fits: a queue or a building project that never ends
idioms.origin: the closing formula of biblical praise (Galatians, Revelation) and of prayers

idioms.text: la oveja perdida / la oveja descarriada
idioms.meaning: someone who has strayed from family or group
idioms.fits: a cousin who stopped coming to Sunday lunch
idioms.origin: Luke 15: a shepherd leaves ninety-nine sheep to find one

idioms.meaning: coming back to family, a group or old habits
idioms.fits: a footballer back at his old club, an ex who returns
idioms.origin: the shepherd and sheep images of Luke 15 and John 10

idioms.text: ama a tu prójimo como a ti mismo
idioms.meaning: treat others as you'd want to be treated
idioms.origin: Leviticus 19, quoted by Jesus in Luke 10

idioms.text: ganarse el pan con el sudor de la frente
idioms.picture: earning bread with the sweat of your brow
idioms.meaning: to earn a living by hard work
idioms.fits: a baker up at 4 a.m., a farmer
idioms.origin: Genesis 3: Adam's punishment on leaving Eden

idioms.meaning: to be cold, unmoved by others' pain
idioms.fits: someone shrugs at a sad story
idioms.origin: Ezekiel 36: a promise to replace hearts of stone with hearts of flesh

idioms.meaning: a place of wild excess and vice
idioms.fits: a wild party, a rowdy nightlife street
idioms.origin: Genesis 19: two cities destroyed for their wickedness

idioms.text: de la abundancia del corazón habla la boca
idioms.picture: the mouth speaks from the heart's overflow
idioms.meaning: what you really feel comes out when you talk
idioms.fits: someone lets slip what they truly think
idioms.origin: Matthew 12, Jesus on words revealing the heart

idioms.text: no se puede servir a dos amos (señores)
idioms.meaning: you can't be loyal to two sides at once
idioms.fits: someone working for two rival shops
idioms.origin: Matthew 6: you can't serve God and money

idioms.text: por sus frutos los conoceréis / al árbol se le conoce por sus frutos
idioms.picture: you'll know them by their fruit
idioms.meaning: judge people by what they do, not what they say
idioms.fits: judging a new boss or a restaurant by results
idioms.origin: Matthew 7 and 12, false prophets and good trees
